title: What Ai are you guys using to develop your Game?
author: AutomaticConnection1
selftext:
I used like 3 Times Claude Ai the Terminal version for Godot, but it runs very fast out of Tickets, are there good Options where you dont pay 1000's of bucks?

  
Would love some recommendations.

comments.author: Odranoel_Altrove
comments.body: I think it mostly depends on the complexity or your project, i used Artifract in Claude but it's a really simple function

comments.author: ponderdiggums
comments.body:
Start with a design document, and implement incrementally. (Use fewer tokens on design) Manually test between implementations and log bugs and design feedback as you go (Use fewer tokens on testing) - if you do automate build deterministic systems where you're interpreting the results instead of the AI. Start with grey boxing, you don't need art and vfx or anything past simpler UI designs at first - come back around to these so you're not dumping tokens into visuals and functionality at the start, make what you can manually (or pay for it) and that should help save some tokens too. 

I use Claude x3 with Unity or Unreal nonstop ~8 hours a day and almost never run out of tokens.

comments.author: overprovisioned_lazy
comments.body:
I believe Claude is relatively cheap. Claude is probably subsidizing users for each request they make (i.e, they are probably losing \~4 times the money you pay for it).  

Some ways to be more token efficient:  
\* Use the agent to write tools for the agent. That way it doesn't need to spend tokens on repetitive tasks. 

But, that will fall over, because agents always go off the rails so:

\* Use the agent to write "guards" for the agent. Dumb scripts or build tooling that "fail loud", and prompt the agent to do the right thing instead. That is more effective and cheaper token wise than trying to write a book of Memory files that will waste tokens on context, and that the agent will ignore half the time anyway.  

\* Use the agent to write tools for you. If there's some repetitive task you're asking the agent to do, get it to write a script to do that thing instead. That way you're not wasting tokens on something that a your computer can do for free.  

Basically, try to be "promoting" things out of the Agent flow, in to a regular code/script flow. Don't go overboard (not everything needs to be s script). But once you notice yourself asking the agent to do the same thing three or more times, consider moving that work flow out of the agent, and in to code.

replies.author: Vindelator
replies.body:
A mess of stuff I haven't entirely figured out yet. 

I've found these sites useful:  
[https://www.pixellab.ai/create-character/new](https://www.pixellab.ai/create-character/new)  
[https://app.spritecook.ai/](https://app.spritecook.ai/)  
[https://collidingscopes.github.io/spritesheet-to-gif/](https://collidingscopes.github.io/spritesheet-to-gif/)

Gemeni can get you some free images to start. Sprite cook can turn things into actual real pixel art from Gemeni (instead of high res images pretending to be pixels) and animate. Pixellab will get 360 views and animations of pixel art characters for an isometric game. 

Obviously, buying assets can work but then your game isn't actually your own style.

comments.author: BenTheSodaman
comments.body:
Started with Cursor while learning, switched to Codex.  
  
But I setup project rules so that the agent doesn't run a headless test/doesn't test, doesn't update every localization each time, and after addressing an issue, occasionally asking it what prompt or project rule would have reached this conclusion sooner, then asking the agent to update the project rule with that solution for future sessions and agents.

While I haven't used Claude yet, I suspect you may have to let it know similarly to not run wild and burn your tokens.

BUT I will say the usage limit on a 0 USD account is wholly insufficient to tackle nearly every idea I would want. I could barely get a Title Screen with a Settings menu out of that allowance. (Settings having audio sliders, adjust keybindings, change resolution and window type with some troubleshooting of that depending on the engine, testing localizations, adjusting and adding input glyphs/legends, other).

comments.author: Nervous_Teach_5596
comments.body:
FREE ONES, ONLY FREE ONES, via chat app in order of use:
DeepSeek (sadly it have lost recently the search on the expert), 
Kimi (This is the only one that has in its version of chat a real "artifact factory", runs Python, creates zip files to download the project and can generate images with Pyplot, especially good for creating maps (mental and simple prototypes), but any LLM can do it with just tell you. Unfortunately, the free one has a chat inference limit, that's the bad part.),
Grok (when it is not yelling at you to pay), 
Google code (I don't have used it in a lot of time because the UI makes my internet and phone tremble),
Google Flow,
Z dot ai GML (recently, I don't have gotten to the actual limit so for now it's pretty resolve captchas because it thinks I'm a robot), 

Why not others:
GPT (the free one generates sentences that don't have more than a line, at the same speed of qwen on cpu inference, and looks like you're reading a poem without sense)
Claude (I can't pass the verification by cell number, so GTFO)


The good part: 0 bucket

The bad part: you will need to do some manual control+c control+v with some thinking, not all automated

 (TLDR: I'm poor, so I can't even pay tokens)

comments.author: LouisGameDevX
comments.body:
Claude Code with Unity MCP has been the best combination for me so far.

One thing that helps with usage is not using the strongest model for everything. I use stronger models for planning, difficult systems and debugging, then something faster for simpler edits.

The workflow also makes a big difference. Work on one focused task at a time, test between changes and start a fresh conversation when the context gets bloated. Asking it to continually reason over the entire game will burn through usage quickly.

comments.author: DuchessCupcakeGames
comments.body:
I use chat gpt painstakingly for assets, sprites, background art, then I formulate a plan, get the game mechanics down, what i want to see, how i want it to work, et cetera on my own, then write a big long prompt to chat gpt/codex and have it put it into a coherent thought and prompt for claude to build a prototype. I take that prototype along with a prompt outline from claude and dump it all into lovable and ask it to make a pwa. The entire process is long but the end result gives me basically what I want, then it's all polishing from there using the same method. I barely use any lovable credits this way and can make a game just with the 5 credits a day lovable gives me. If I'm really into an idea and want to finish it quickly, I buy a subscription plan for lovable and then cancel it to the 5 dollar a month plan so I can keep all my domains there. Ultimately I'm planning to house everything on github, but I'm having too much fun making little improvements every day and 5 bucks a month is nothing. I pour in the dough when I want something really good because that prototype process, while it gives you a working model, it's never really all that great until you add your png assets and what not.
